Congratulations to the Hoover Institution's Robert E. Hall, on His Economics Nobel Prize
From Hoover's post today (and see also our colleague John Cochrane's post about Hall's work):
Robert E. Hall, the Robert and Carole McNeil Endowed Professor in Economics and Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution, Emeritus, and emeritus professor of economics in the School of Humanities and Sciences, is the recipient of the 2026 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.
Hall was recognized with the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel for his contributions to the "microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization," alongside economist Michael Woodford, with whom he will share the approximately $1.2 million prize.
"Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are awarded this year's prize in economic sciences for demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy," according to an announcement from the Nobel Committee. "Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation. This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions."
"This is a wonderful surprise," Hall said on Monday morning. "I've spent my career trying to understand how the economy works, following interesting questions wherever they led. When I thought I had a new idea, the next step was to find out whether it was actually new, whether it was right, and whether it mattered. I've been fortunate to have extraordinary colleagues and coauthors to help me sort that out, and working with them has been the greatest pleasure of my career."
Robert E. Hall, 83, is a member of the National Academy of Sciences and a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, the Econometric Society and the Society of Labor Economists. Hall is an applied economist with interests in technology, competition, employment issues, and economic policy. He is a frequent contributor to discussions of national economic policy, including monetary policy, fiscal policy, and competition policy. Hall's research focuses on levels of activity and stock market valuations in market economies and on the economics of high technology, particularly the Internet.
Bob Hall is one of the most distinguished economists of his generation, whose work has profoundly shaped our understanding of economic growth, employment, and the forces that drive the American economy," said Hoover Institution Director Condoleezza Rice. "He has been instrumental in the way policy leaders think about the free market economy. This great honor is a well deserved recognition of a remarkable career, and we at Hoover are proud to call him a colleague.
"Bob Hall's creative and impactful work illuminates the connections between how households and firms behave and the outcomes of the economy as a whole, said Stanford President Jonathan Levin. "His insights have changed how governments and central banks respond to economic volatility. I'm thrilled that he has been honored with this year's Nobel Prize in Economics."
"Hall has made pioneering contributions to our understanding of household consumption, employment fluctuations, and market power," said Debra Satz, the Vernon R. and Lysbeth Warren Anderson Dean of the School of Humanities and Sciences. "It is wonderful to see his lifetime of work in applied economics recognized by the Nobel committee."
Along with Hoover colleague Alvin Rabushka, Hall is an active proponent of the flat tax. Their article in the Wall Street Journal in December 1981 was the starting point of an upsurge of interest in the flat tax. This led to their book, The Flat Tax. The pair was recognized in Money magazine's Money Hall of Fame for their contributions to financial innovation over the past twenty years.
Hall also serves as director of the research program on economic fluctuations and growth of the National Bureau of Economic Research, an interuniversity research organization. He is chairman of the bureau's Committee on Business Cycle Dating, which maintains the semiofficial chronology of the US business cycle.
Hall has advised a number of government agencies on national economic policy, including the Justice Department, the Treasury Department, and the Federal Reserve Board. He served on President-elect Ronald Reagan's Task Force on Inflation Policy and was a member of the National Presidential Advisory Committee on Productivity. He has testified on numerous occasions before congressional committees concerning national economic policy. He presented the Ely Lecture to the American Economic Association in 2001.
Before coming to Stanford, Hall was a professor of economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and an assistant professor at the University of California at Berkeley.
Born in Palo Alto, California, he attended school in Palo Alto and Los Angeles, received his BA from the University of California at Berkeley and his PhD from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Hall is married to economist Susan Woodward and lives in Menlo Park, California.
"Stanford's Economics Department and the Hoover Institution gave me a dream job: the freedom and time to do the research I wanted to do," Hall said. "The taxpayers of California gave me an excellent education in the public schools and at Berkeley, and the federal government paid for my graduate education at MIT. I hope they will regard this as a satisfactory return on their investment. I thank my family, especially my wonderful wife and coauthor, Susan, and congratulate Michael Woodford, whose work has taught me a great deal."

2 U.S. economists win Nobel prize for work on economic stability
STOCKHOLM >> U.S. academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize on Monday for decades of work developing ground-up models currently used by central banks and finance ministries across the world to stabilise economies.
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.
Woodford and Hall are frequently name-checked by the world’s top central banks, which after a 2022 inflation surge in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, are currently grappling with the energy shock triggered by the Iran war.
One of the laureates’ key insights is that economies could only be kept on an even keel by taking into account the millions of decisions made at a micro-level by households and businesses, rather than by using top-down theories of how economies work.
“… Authorities shouldn’t view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy independently of what people in the economy understand about this,” Columbia University’s Woodford, 70, told a news conference.
In contrast to the oil shocks of the 1970s, when central banks struggled to combat sky-high inflation, Woodford said the new framework was useful during the global financial crisis of the late-2000s to bolster traditional tools of monetary policy.

“Making more explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rate policy, as opposed to relying on simply being able to cut interest rates further immediately, that was an important part of the policy response in the years from 2009 onward,” he said.
Beyond so-called “forward guidance” on the future path of monetary policy, the work of Woodford — and Hall, 83, at Stanford University — promoted other concepts used today such as the idea of “sticky” inflation when price changes lag changes in demand.
Another is the “output gap,” a measure of demand pressure building up in an economy and how efficiently resources are being used — the goal of stabilisation policy being to steer that gap towards zero.
Hall has served as adviser to the U.S. Treasury Department, the Justice Department and the Federal Reserve Board.
His insight in a 1978 paper that household decisions on consumption are a perfect indicator of their expectations was used by Woodford in a model on how consumption is determined.
Woodford also showed that central banks can stimulate or suppress economic activity by adjusting interest rates, rather than just by the amount of money in circulation.
Such concepts remain core to central banking today. Forward guidance became especially important after the 2008 financial crisis, when rates were near zero or even negative and standard monetary policy seemed to be out of ammunition.
Now, however, some are questioning how relevant it is given the amount of uncertainty in the global economy — with new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh a notable sceptic.
The economics prize, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final award to be given out this year and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).
First awarded in 1969, it is not one of the original five awards created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was established by Sweden’s central bank.
The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States.
Last year’s winners, Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt, won for work on “creative destruction” and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards.
The Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace were announced last week.
Reporting by Simon Johnson, Niklas Pollard, Johan Ahlander and Marie Mannes in Stockholm, Terje Solsvik in Oslo, Mark John in London.

sources.news_title: Hall And Woodford Win Economics Nobel For Research On Economic Stability
sources.text:
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences on Monday for research that helps governments and central banks respond to recessions, inflation and other economic shocks.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the October 12 award to Hall, of Stanford University, and Woodford, of Columbia University, “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” They will split 12 million Swedish kronor equally.
Their work helped rebuild economic models around the decisions that households and businesses make, including how much to spend, save and charge for goods. The academy said those models improved policymakers’ ability to limit economic swings.
“It’s a tremendous honor. It’s a surprise. But I’m feeling very good about it,” Woodford said by phone during the announcement, according to Columbia University’s account.
The research addresses a practical problem: People and businesses act on what they expect tomorrow, not simply what they earn or pay today.
Hall developed a way to test how expectations about future income shape household spending. His work also gave researchers a benchmark for studying households that cannot borrow or lack savings, the academy explained.
Woodford brought household spending and business pricing decisions into a model that helps policymakers examine how interest-rate changes affect the economy. He presented the model in a 2003 book.
The framework also highlights why central banks communicate their plans. Expectations about future rates and costs can influence what households buy and what businesses charge now.
Central banks and finance ministries around the world use models that build on this research, according to the academy. Researchers continue to refine them as economies change.
Sweden’s central bank established the economics memorial prize in 1968 to mark its 300th anniversary. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences selects recipients under the same principles that govern the Nobel Prizes, according to Columbia.

sources.news_title: The economics Nobel went to the scholar whose work shaped Fed 'forward guidance,' a practice Kevin Warsh says has gone too far
sources.text:
American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks, such as energy crises and inflation.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, noting that their work created the theoretical foundation to better understand how consumers decide whether to save or spend, insights that make it easier for policymakers worldwide to stabilize economies after fluctuations.
“The laureates’ research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before,” the Nobel committee wrote in a paper explaining the economists’ work. “It has been hugely beneficial during the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years.”
Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York.
Woodford spoke to the committee by phone from New York: “It’s a tremendous honor. It’s a surprise.”
Duo overturned earlier economic assumptions
For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: Intervene in the economy by lowering interest rates and taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest and help restart growth.
“This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn’t,” said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics committee.
Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple trade-offs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the “ stagflation ’’ of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic.
Some economists argued that government attempts to intervene in the economy were doomed to fail. But Hall and Woodford, in separate contributions, set about improving the Keynesian model to take into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend.
“Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,’’ the Nobel committee wrote. “Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird’s eye view,” Hall and Woodford’s research “generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilization policy.”
Hall studied consumer choices
Hall studied the way that consumers’ decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be.
“If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,’’ the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. Hall found that forecasting future consumer spending is virtually impossible.
The idea that consumption is mostly unpredictable “is not good news for forecasters, or policymakers,” Olivier Blanchard, who was chief economist at the International Monetary Fund during the 2008 financial crisis, said by email. “But it is news they must take into account in thinking about the effects of policy.”
Hall also explored the idea that some households are so strapped financially that they can’t borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes. In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80% of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future “while the rest lived hand to mouth,” the committee wrote.
“The prize is for research that pushes our understanding of macroeconomics from the bottom up, from families and firms making decisions over time, while looking ahead,” Ivan Werning, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said in an email.
Woodford analyzed how businesses make decisions
Woodford’s research established that businesses make decisions about prices based on where they think interest rates will go in the future.
“If the business believes that its competitors’ prices and its own costs will increase, it is best to set a higher price than it would with the opposite expectation,” the Nobel committee wrote. “Businesses’ decisions are thus also governed by their expectations.”
Therefore, central banks such as the U.S. Federal Reserve, which set short-term interest rates, should provide “clear and credible communication about how they reason and what they plan to do.” Central banks have responded to this insight by working harder to explain what they are doing.
The new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, has said the trend toward such “forward guidance” went too far. He’s trying to scale back how much the U.S. central bank talks about its thinking and its intentions.
Woodford’s research also offered guidance on how central banks should respond to energy price shocks — like the one that followed the U.S. and Israeli attack on Iran in February — that can both feed inflation and send unemployment higher.
“Unlike the traditional Keynesian models, Woodford’s model recommends a cooling measure, such as increased interest rates, to avoid uncontrolled inflation,” the Nobel committee wrote. “His insight has made it possible to respond to recent supply shocks more effectively than during the oil crises of the 1970s.”
During the phone call broadcast at a news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed “the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending.”
Economics prize is last Nobel announcement this year
The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.
Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896.
Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.
Monday’s award was the second Nobel win for a Stanford University professor this year. Dr. Karl Deisseroth shared the medicine prize with Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work that led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.
___
Dazio reported from Berlin, and Wiseman reported from Washington. Associated Press Writer Wyatte Grantham-Philips in Chicago contributed to this report.

Two U.S. economists win Nobel for work incorporating consumers’ views into boom-bust predictions
This year’s prize highlights Robert Hall and Michael Woodford’s work developing models that take future expectations of the public into account in economic policy
Marta Zherukha • October 12, 2026
An illustration of Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, winners of the 2026 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. [Credit: Niklas Elmehed © Nobel Prize Outreach]
Two U.S. economists won the 2026 Nobel Prize today in economics for creating new models that help stabilize countries in tough financial times.
Robert Hall and Michael Woodford updated a classic economic theory after the 1970s oil crisis, restructuring the question of supply and demand to also include consumer expectations. The old theory by John Maynard Keynes was “a black, unreliable box,” said Timo Boppart, a member of the prize committee.
While the old theory looks exclusively at high-level economic decisions, how governments could intervene via taxes and spending, he said, the new one takes decisions by individual households and businesses into account. This smooths out bumps in the economy by understanding actual consumer behavior instead of relying on top-down statistics.
“Disposable income matters, but also the entire future path of income is relevant, too,” Boppart added. “If consumers see dark clouds on the horizon, they cut back on consumption.”
Hall studied consumption, and he found a way to quantify its theories. In 1978, he reasoned that if consumption is based on all past choices, changes only happen with new information. So, changes in consumer behavior are unpredictable.
Boppart used an illustrated ice cream menu to explain Woodford’s part of the theory: how people spend money and how businesses set prices. In this analogy, the microeconomic foundation is how much people are willing to pay for a summer treat. That foundation sits under the overarching goal of macroeconomic stabilization — how much the truck can reasonably charge for one.
Under the old Keynesian framework, the ice cream truck driver keeps the price the same each year without considering a change in supply or demand. Under the new framework, the driver adjusts prices early in the summer based on predictions like weather forecasts and tourist numbers.
“Price-setting becomes forward looking,” Boppart said. “If you know that the price of your ice cream is gonna last for the whole season, you better look ahead when you set it in the first place.”
Woodford said his work stresses the importance of government transparency when making economic policy. According to him, people understanding the future of their financial decisions is crucial to those policies actually working.
“Government authorities shouldn’t view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy independently of what people in the economy understand about this,” Woodford said in a phone call with the prize committee.
Hall teaches applied economics at Stanford University, and Woodford teaches political economy at Columbia University.
Hall and Woodford won 12 million Swedish kronor (almost $1.2 million), which will be split equally between them. The economics award wasn’t in Alfred Nobel’s will, so it isn’t technically a Nobel prize. It was added to the original set by Sweden’s central bank to celebrate its 300th anniversary in 1968.
In a press conference Monday morning, Woodford referenced the 2008 financial crisis as a key period when traditional tools like Keynes’s weren’t enough to restore economic activity.
The conventional path was to cut interest rates to stimulate spending, which happened in the U.S. and other countries around the world. However, rates remained at basically zero by the end of the year while spending remained low and unemployment high. Governments had to try something different.
The new theory helped deal with the problem by asking governments and banks to be more transparent about the likely future path of that policy. Woodford said forward looking contributed to better stabilization.
Hall’s and Woodford’s framework is also helpful in challenging times brought on by non-economic events, like the Iran-U.S. War that has disrupted the energy market.
“It makes me very excited to see this core macroeconomic topic being rewarded with a prize,” Boppart said.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, saying the two were being honored for work that has helped policymakers deal with economic fluctuations.
“The laureates’ research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before,” the Nobel committee wrote. “It has been hugely beneficial during the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years.″
Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York.
Woodford spoke to the committee by phone Monday from New York, saying: “It’s a tremendous honor, it’s a surprise.”
The Nobel committee said the laureates’ work has created the theoretical foundation for models now used by central banks and governments around the world.
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a news release.
The 2 overturned earlier economic assumptions
For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest and help restart growth.
“This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn’t,’’ said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics prize committee. Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple trade-offs – unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the “stagflation’’ of the 1970s – when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment – proved the formula was simplistic.
Some economists argued that government attempts to intervene in the economy were doomed to fail. But Hall and Woodford, in separate contributions, set about improving the Keynesian model to take into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend.
“Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,’’ the Nobel committee wrote. “Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird’s eye view, Hall’s and Woodford’s research has generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilization policy.’’
Hall studied consumer decisions
Hall studied the way that consumers’ decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be.
“If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,’’ the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. And some households are so poor they can’t borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes.
In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80% of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future “while the rest lived hand to mouth,’’ the committee wrote.
Woodford analyzed how businesses make decisions
Woodford’s research established that businesses make decisions about prices based on where they think interest rates will go in the future. “If the business believes that its competitors’ prices and its own costs will increase, it is best to set a higher price than it would with the opposite expectation,” the Nobel committee wrote. “Businesses’ decisions are thus also governed by their expectations.’’
Therefore, central banks such as the U.S. Federal Reserve, which set short-term interest rates, should provide “clear and credible communication about how they reason and what they plan to do.’’ Central banks have responded to this insight by working harder to explain what they are doing.
During the phone call broadcast at the news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed “the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending.”
The economics prize is the last Nobel announcement this year
Last year, three researchers who study business innovation won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies in the dust.
The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.
Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896.
Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.
Monday’s award was the second Nobel win for a Stanford University professor this year. Dr. Karl Deisseroth shared the medicine prize with Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work that led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.

sources.text:
The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for 2026 goes to two American academics - Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford - "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."
This year's laureates are macroeconomist and monetary theorist Michael Dean Woodford, and economist Robert Hall.
They have developed new macroeconomic models that have significantly helped improve the ability to implement effective stabilization policy. On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy's peaks and troughs.
The economy is characterized by alternating downturns and upturns. Ever since the economist John Maynard Keynes launched his theories almost a century ago, stabilization policy has been important for tackling these fluctuations. During recessions, the economy is boosted by reducing interest rates and increasing the budget deficit, while the opposite should be done to slow a booming economy.
However, during the oil crises of the 1970s, it seemed that the Keynesian models that govern when and how measures should be implemented no longer worked. They did not reduce unemployment, but led to uncontrolled inflation instead. The West experienced a decade of low growth, high unemployment and high inflation. Many people believed that stabilization policy had done more harm than good and that it should be retired.
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are awarded this year's prize in economic sciences for demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalize stabilization policy. Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation. This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.
|  | 
A central component in these models is that households and businesses are forward looking when making decisions about savings or product prices. When governments and central banks communicate their plans for economic policy, they can influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction. "Since the new models' introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us," the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.
"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," says John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.
Robert Hall, 83, is Professor at Stanford University, CA.
Michael Woodford, 71, is a Professor at Columbia University, New York.
The prize amount of 12 million Swedish kronor, or 11,97,646, will be shared equally between the laureates.

‘New Keynesian’ economists win Nobel prize
Two American economists who research price stabilisation across global economies have won the Nobel prize for economics.
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford were the joint winners of the prestigious award officially called “The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel”.
Hall and Woodford’s research on forecasting has influenced policymakers when setting interest rates or announcing spending packages.
Woodford is widely credited for laying the foundations on so-called “forward guidance” used by central banks to signal whether interest rates may rise. Hall is also known for creating the ‘fresh-water and salt-water’ divide in economics, contrasting free-market views with those who believe governments and central banks should take a more active role in the economy
The pair, who will claim the award worth £900,000, are considered to be part of the ‘New Keynesian’ tradition, a school of thought that develops ideas built by the British economist John Maynard Keynes.
New Keynesian modelling explains how a string of individual household and business decisions can create wider economic effects, including the slow pass-through of market imperfections into prices and wages. The school of thought revisits ideas by Keynes amid previous assumptions that era of high inflation would lead to lower unemployment.
Nobel prize for ‘shift in stabilisation policy’
Explaining the decision for the award, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockhold said: “Economic development is characterised by alternating downturns and upturns. Stimulating or slowing down the economy at the right time can provide stability and allow us to avoid drawn-out recessions or runaway inflation. Robert E. Hall’s and Michael Woodford’s research has generated a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy.”
“New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world.”
Last year, Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt won the Nobel prize for economics for their research on growth by technological progress and “creative destruction”, whereby progress and the development of welfare relies on new innovations replacing older technologies.
The Nobel peace prize this year went to Navi Pillay, an International Criminal Court judge who has written reports on war crimes in the Hamas-Israel war and investigated the Rwandan genocide.

Americans Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel economics prize Monday for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can better stabilise disruptive economic fluctuations.
The two were honoured for developing new models for managing recessions and other crises that fail to respond to traditional tools.
"On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy's peaks and troughs," the jury said.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences explained in a statement that ever since John Maynard Keynes formulated his economic theories almost a century ago, "stabilisation" policies had long let officials boost economic growth when needed.
But during the oil shocks in the 1970s, the Keynesian models that governed when and how action should be taken no longer worked.
Hall, 83, a professor at Stanford University, and Woodford, a professor at Columbia University born in 1955, separately began to explore new models.
"Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation," the jury said.
Hall and Woodford's models include an "understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions", it said.
A fundamental aspect of this is the understanding that households are forward-looking when making decisions about spending or saving.
This means the way governments and central banks communicate their policies can influence people's views of the future when making such decisions.
"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, chair of the prize-awarding committee, said in a statement.
"It's a surprise, but I'm feeling very good about it," Woodford told reporters via phone during the announcement of the prize, saying he felt "elated" over receiving "a tremendous honour".

One of the new approaches employed by central banks was to start making "more explicit statements" on where they believed guiding interest rates were headed in the future, which continues to this day.
"I think it did contribute to better stabilisation. It didn't magically solve the problem, but I think it was an important contribution," Woodford said.

STOCKHOLM (AP) — American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel memorial prize in economics on Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks, such as energy crises and inflation.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, saying the two were being honored for work that has helped policymakers deal with economic fluctuations.
“The laureates’ research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before,” the Nobel committee wrote. “It has been hugely beneficial during the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years.″
Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York.
Woodford spoke to the committee by phone Monday from New York, saying: “It’s a tremendous honor, it’s a surprise.”
The Nobel committee said the laureates’ work has created the theoretical foundation for models now used by central banks and governments around the world.
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a news release.
The 2 overturned earlier economic assumptions
For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest and help restart growth.
“This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn’t,’’ said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics prize committee. Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple trade-offs – unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the “stagflation’’ of the 1970s – when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment – proved the formula was simplistic.
Some economists argued that government attempts to intervene in the economy were doomed to fail. But Hall and Woodford, in separate contributions, set about improving the Keynesian model to take into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend.
“Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,’’ the Nobel committee wrote. “Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird’s eye view, Hall’s and Woodford’s research has generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilization policy.’’
Hall studied consumer decisions
Hall studied the way that consumers’ decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be.
“If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,’’ the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. And some households are so poor they can’t borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes.
In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80% of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future “while the rest lived hand to mouth,’’ the committee wrote.
Woodford analyzed how businesses make decisions
Woodford’s research established that businesses make decisions about prices based on where they think interest rates will go in the future. “If the business believes that its competitors’ prices and its own costs will increase, it is best to set a higher price than it would with the opposite expectation,” the Nobel committee wrote. “Businesses’ decisions are thus also governed by their expectations.’’
Therefore, central banks such as the U.S. Federal Reserve, which set short-term interest rates, should provide “clear and credible communication about how they reason and what they plan to do.’’ Central banks have responded to this insight by working harder to explain what they are doing.
During the phone call broadcast at the news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed “the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending.”
The economics prize is the last Nobel announcement this year
Last year, three researchers who study business innovation won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies in the dust.
The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes.
Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896.
Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace.
Monday’s award was the second Nobel win for a Stanford University professor this year. Dr. Karl Deisseroth shared the medicine prize with Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work that led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

The economics Nobel Prize went Monday to Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, recognizing research that rebuilt the foundations of policies used to manage economic fluctuations. The academy honored them “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation,” according to its official award announcement. Their work places the decisions of households and businesses inside models of the wider economy, rather than relying only on statistical relationships among measures such as inflation, production and consumption.
A central element is that people and companies look ahead when deciding how much to save or what prices to charge. The academy said governments and central banks can influence those expectations by communicating their policy plans. It described the models as a foundation for responding to disturbances including energy crises and changes in household consumption.
The intellectual problem emerged sharply during the oil crises of the 1970s, when economies experienced weak growth, unemployment and inflation together. Euronews, in its account of Monday’s announcement, described how the failure of earlier Keynesian models encouraged the development of different tools for assessing policy responses. Hall and Woodford’s contributions were part of that reconstruction.
Hall’s career has encompassed both academic research and work with institutions concerned with national economic policy. In his Stanford biography, he describes himself as an applied economist whose interests include employment, inflation, technology and competition. Those interests extend across the aggregate economy and individual markets.
He received his undergraduate degree from the University of California, Berkeley, and his doctorate from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Before joining Stanford’s Hoover Institution and economics department in 1978, he taught at MIT and Berkeley. His university site identifies him as the Robert and Carole McNeil Joint Hoover Senior Fellow and Professor of Economics.
Hall served as president of the American Economic Association in 2010, following service as vice president in 2005 and the association’s distinguished lecture in 2001. His biography also records advice to the Justice Department, Treasury, Federal Reserve Board and Congressional Budget Office. He directed the National Bureau of Economic Research’s program on economic fluctuations and growth from 1978 through 2013.
The publication record on Hall’s Stanford site spans decades of questions about how people work, consume and respond to policy. It lists “The Dynamic Effects of Fiscal Policy in an Economy with Foresight,” published in the Review of Economic Studies in 1971, and “Stochastic Implications of the Life Cycle-Permanent Income Hypothesis: Theory and Evidence,” published in the Journal of Political Economy in December 1978.
Later entries include “Fiscal Stimulus,” published in Daedalus in 2010, and “The Long Slump,” his 2011 American Economic Association presidential address. His work has also continued into labor-market research: the list includes “The Inexorable Recoveries of US Unemployment,” written with Marianna Kudlyak and published in the Journal of Monetary Economics in 2022. These are separate publications across his career, rather than a list of findings announced with Monday’s prize.
Woodford’s academic training took a different route before reaching the same doctoral institution. Columbia’s biography says he earned an undergraduate degree at the University of Chicago, a law degree at Yale Law School and a doctorate in economics at MIT. He is Columbia’s John Bates Clark Professor of Political Economy.
His earlier honors include the Deutsche Bank Prize in Financial Economics in 2007, the Banque de France/Toulouse School of Economics Prize in Monetary Economics in 2018 and the Erwin Plein Nemmers Prize in Economics in 2024. Columbia also records that he has been a MacArthur Fellow and a Guggenheim Fellow. His research affiliations include the NBER and the Centre for Economic Policy Research.
The university identifies “Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy” as his principal treatise. It also lists his participation in the “Handbook of Macroeconomics,” the “Handbook of Monetary Economics” and “The Inflation Targeting Debate.” His current research, according to the biography, examines bounded rationality, including decisions made with imprecise mental representations and findings from psychology and neuroscience.

Its published description sets out the problem of managing fiat currencies when monetary policy is not organized around commodity backing or a target for the growth of the money supply.

Later chapters address welfare, commitment to a policy rule and the design of optimal monetary-policy rules. The framework treats the evaluation of policy as a question about economic outcomes and objectives, rather than only the setting of an instrument.
Household expectations remain a subject of direct measurement as well as theory. The New York Federal Reserve’s September Survey of Consumer Expectations, released October 7, found median one-year-ahead inflation expectations at 3.9 percent. The three-year reading was 3.3 percent, while the five-year reading remained at 3 percent.
The survey was conducted from September 1 through September 30. Its findings concern what households anticipated, rather than the price increases actually recorded during that month. FINCHANNEL’s October report on inflation expectations examined that distinction between respondents’ outlook and measured inflation.
The same September survey put expected household income growth at 3.1 percent and expected spending growth at 5.5 percent. Those figures describe anticipated growth, not income and purchases already recorded.
The New York Fed describes the survey as a nationally representative internet panel of about 1,300 household heads. Participants remain in the panel for up to 12 months, with a roughly equal number entering and leaving each month. That design allows researchers to observe changes in the expectations of the same individuals over time.
The award’s formal name is the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The Swedish central bank established it in 1968, at its 300th anniversary, according to the academy’s account of the prize. Economics was not among the five prizes created in Alfred Nobel’s will.
The academy announces the economics laureates in October, after they have been selected. The award ceremony takes place on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death. Last year’s economics award went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for research on technology and growth, Euronews reported in its account of the new award.
The academy’s economics prize committee investigates and evaluates nominees, but the academy as a whole makes the award decision. Its published rules say no more than three people may share the prize. Nominations come through invitations to selected scholars, academy members and previous economics laureates, with international experts helping assess specific research contributions.
Who won the 2026 economics Nobel Prize?
Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University.
What research was recognized?
The microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization, including how household and business decisions enter models used to analyze policy.
How much is the award?
The laureates will share 12 million Swedish kronor equally.

U.S. academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize on Monday for decades of work developing ground-up models currently used by central banks and finance ministries across the world to stabilize economies.

One of the laureates’ key insights is that economies could only be kept on an even keel by taking into account the millions of decisions made at a micro-level by households and businesses, rather than by using top-down theories of how economies work.
“... Authorities shouldn’t view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy independently of what people in the economy understand about this,” Columbia University’s Woodford, 70, told a news conference.
In contrast to the oil shocks of the 1970s, when central banks struggled to combat sky-high inflation, Woodford said the new framework was useful during the global financial crisis of the late-2000s to bolster traditional tools of monetary policy.
“Making more explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rate policy, as opposed to relying on simply being able to cut interest rates further immediately, that was an important part of the policy response in the years from 2009 onward,” he said.
Beyond so-called “forward guidance” on the future path of monetary policy, the work of Woodford – and Hall, 83, at Stanford University – promoted other concepts used today such as the idea of “sticky” inflation when price changes lag changes in demand.
Another is the “output gap,” a measure of demand pressure building up in an economy and how efficiently resources are being used – the goal of stabilization policy being to steer that gap towards zero.
Core central bank concepts
Hall has served as adviser to the U.S. Treasury Department, the Justice Department and the Federal Reserve Board.
His insight in a 1978 paper that household decisions on consumption are a perfect indicator of their expectations was used by Woodford in a model on how consumption is determined.
Hall called the prize “a wonderful surprise” in a statement.
“I’ve spent my career trying to understand how the economy works,” he said. “When I thought I had a new idea, the next step was to find out whether it was actually new, whether it was right, and whether it mattered.”
Woodford also showed that central banks can stimulate or suppress economic activity by adjusting interest rates, rather than just by the amount of money in circulation.
Such concepts remain core to central banking today. Forward guidance became especially important after the 2008 financial crisis, when rates were near zero or even negative and standard monetary policy seemed to be out of ammunition.
Now, however, some are questioning how relevant it is given the amount of uncertainty in the global economy – with new U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh a notable skeptic.
The economics prize, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final award to be given out this year and is worth 12-million Swedish crowns (US$1.2-million).
First awarded in 1969, it is not one of the original five awards created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was established by Sweden’s central bank.
The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States.
Last year’s winners, Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt, won for work on “creative destruction” and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards.
The Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace were announced last week.

Two Americans have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on how to smooth boom-and-bust cycles to limit inflation and unemployment.
Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University were honored for their focus on how individual households and businesses make decisions on purchases and pricing — work that became the foundation of the "New Keynesian" approach to economics.
The importance of that work has been underscored in recent years by the pandemic, which pushed millions of people out of work, and the supply shocks that followed, driving up the cost of living.
"Regardless of the causes, an important goal for governments and central banks is to reduce the amplitude of these swings and limit the risk that the economy gets stuck in a situation with high unemployment or loses control over inflation," said John Hassler, the chairman of the economic prize committee. This award is not one of the original five, but a "memorial" prize that honors Alfred Nobel.
After the Great Depression, John Maynard Keynes persuaded policymakers that government sometimes needed to stimulate demand during downturns to curb unemployment, or tamp down demand during boom times to limit inflation.
"This is the Keynesian recipe, and it worked well until it didn't," said Tim Boppart, a member of the prize committee. In the 1970s, the economy was hit by rising unemployment and inflation simultaneously.
"The Keynesian recipe was shattered," Boppart says. Hall and Woodford added some necessary ingredients, focusing on the individual households and businesses that help shape the larger economy.
Hall concentrated on demand and how households make purchasing decisions, guided not only by current purchasing power but what they expect their incomes will be in the future.
"If consumers see dark clouds on the horizon, they cut back on consumption already today," Boppart says.
Woodford focused on the supply side and how businesses set prices. Here again, expectations are key. Historically, it was costly to change prices, so businesses try to think ahead and set prices that would cover costs for an extended period.
Because both households and businesses are forward-looking, the Nobel laureates argued, policymakers should communicate their plans clearly to the public.
"One of the themes in my work is that government authorities shouldn't view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy, independent of what people in the economy understand," Woodford told reporters after the prize was announced.
Woodford says tools intended to smooth out boom-and-bust cycles work better when people know what the government is trying to accomplish, and he urged policymakers to talk directly to the public about "why the things that are being done are being done."

American economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford have been awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for developing models that show how monetary and fiscal policy can better stabilise disruptive economic fluctuations. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the prize, honouring the two researchers for creating new frameworks to manage recessions and crises that do not respond to traditional policy tools.
The academy said the laureates’ work provides a stable theoretical foundation for the models now used by central banks and governments worldwide. Hall, 83, a professor at Stanford University, and Woodford, a professor at Columbia University, separately began exploring new approaches after the Keynesian models that had guided policy since the early 20th century failed during the oil shocks of the 1970s. Rather than relying on statistical links between macroeconomic variables such as inflation, production and consumption, they built their models on a microeconomic foundation. This approach incorporates an understanding of how the collective actions of forward-looking households and businesses affect the Economy.
A fundamental aspect of their research is the recognition that households make spending and saving decisions based on expectations of the future. This means the way governments and central banks communicate their policies can influence those expectations and, consequently, economic behaviour. “On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the jury said.
John Hassler, chair of the prize-awarding committee, stated that the laureates’ work underpins the models currently employed by policymakers globally. Woodford, reached by phone during the announcement, described the award as a tremendous honour. He cited the 2008 financial crisis as a concrete example of their research in practice. When interest rates had been lowered to zero in many countries, traditional monetary tools were inadequate. Central banks responded by issuing more explicit statements about the future path of rates — a strategy known as forward guidance — which Woodford said contributed to better stabilisation, though it did not magically solve the problem.
Woodford emphasised that his theories were not motivated by a specific political agenda but by an attempt to improve the foundations for economic policy discussion and public understanding. The prize, which includes a diploma, a gold medal and 1.2 million dollars, recognises a body of work that has reshaped how policymakers approach economic stability in an era of complex challenges.
